title: Where history meets the story of origins
paragraphs: Among the most enduring narratives associated with the beginnings of Korea is the story of Dangun. It is commonly retold as an origin account for Gojoseon, but its significance extends beyond any straightforward question of whether a particular founding event happened in the form described. The story matters because communities have returned to it repeatedly to explain antiquity, belonging, legitimacy, and the relationship between the human world and a sacred or extraordinary past.

A foundation narrative is not the same object as a contemporary administrative record. Stories travel through time. They are shaped by transmission, preservation, selection, and reinterpretation. A text written down centuries after the period it describes can be an excellent source for understanding the beliefs and cultural memory of the time when it circulated, while still being an uncertain guide to the much earlier events it appears to recount.

This distinction does not make the tale historically unimportant. On the contrary, it makes possible several different histories at once: the history of the story, the history of its preservation, the history of changing interpretations, and the separate archaeological problem of reconstructing early societies on the peninsula and in neighboring regions.
